what_are_dreams.title: Why We Dream
what_are_dreams.summary: Science does not yet have one proven answer. Leading ideas connect dreaming with memory, emotion, learning, and the brain’s ongoing construction of experience.
what_are_dreams.source_title: The Functional Role of Dreaming in Emotional Processes

what_are_dreams.title: REM Sleep
what_are_dreams.summary: REM dreams are often longer, more vivid, emotional, and story-like, but dreaming is not limited to REM sleep.
what_are_dreams.source_title: Structural differences between REM and non-REM dream reports

what_are_dreams.title: Non-REM Dreams
what_are_dreams.summary: People also dream during non-REM sleep. Reports are often shorter and less vivid on average, although meaningful and complex non-REM dreams do occur.

what_are_dreams.title: Why Dreams Are Forgotten
what_are_dreams.summary: Dream recall varies greatly. Timing of awakening, attention, sleep stage, memory abilities, and personal interest can all affect what is remembered.
what_are_dreams.source_title: Spotlight on dream recall: the ages of dreams

what_are_dreams.title: False Awakenings
what_are_dreams.summary: A false awakening is a dream in which you believe you have awakened and begun normal activities, only to discover that you are still dreaming.

what_are_dreams.title: Lucid Dreaming
what_are_dreams.summary: A lucid dream occurs when a person becomes aware that they are dreaming while the dream is still happening. Control may be present, but awareness is the defining feature.
what_are_dreams.source_title: The cognitive neuroscience of lucid dreaming

what_are_dreams.title: Nightmares
what_are_dreams.summary: Nightmares are distressing dreams that commonly involve threat, fear, or helplessness. Frequent nightmares that disrupt daily life may deserve professional attention.

what_are_dreams.title: Recurring Dreams
what_are_dreams.summary: Recurring dreams repeat a storyline, setting, emotion, or theme. Recording changes in the dream and waking-life circumstances can reveal personal patterns.

history.title: Ancient Egypt
history.summary: Surviving Egyptian dream texts include lists of dream images and proposed outcomes. These records show that interpretation was embedded in the religion and social assumptions of its own period.

history.title: Ancient Greece
history.summary: Greek traditions included divine messages, healing dreams at sanctuaries, philosophical debate, and systematic interpretation such as Artemidorus’s later dream manual.

history.title: Ancient Rome
history.summary: Roman accounts often treated dreams as possible omens, political warnings, personal messages, or subjects for skeptical analysis, depending on author and period.

history.title: Biblical Traditions
history.summary: Biblical narratives contain dreams connected with warning, guidance, kingship, survival, and interpretation. Somneiros presents these as religious and literary traditions, not universal proof of prophecy.

history.title: Islamic Scholarship
history.summary: Islamic traditions developed careful categories for dreams and extensive interpretive literature. Material must be tied to specific scholars and texts rather than reduced to generic symbolism.

history.title: Medieval Europe
history.summary: Medieval European writers debated whether dreams arose from bodily conditions, everyday concerns, spiritual influence, or deception. Interpretation varied across medicine, theology, and folklore.

history.title: Indigenous Traditions
history.summary: There is no single Indigenous dream system. Any entry must identify the specific community, source, language, and permission context, and avoid combining distinct peoples into one tradition.

history.title: Modern Psychology
history.summary: Freud and Jung made dreams central to influential psychological theories. Their interpretations remain historically important, but many claims are debated and should not be presented as settled science.

history.title: Contemporary Sleep Science
history.summary: Modern research studies dream reports, brain activity, sleep stages, memory, emotion, and consciousness. It does not support a universal dictionary in which every symbol has one fixed meaning.

famous_dreams.title: August Kekulé
famous_dreams.claim: Kekulé later described a reverie or dreamlike vision of a snake biting its tail while thinking about benzene’s ring structure.
famous_dreams.status: Later first-person account; details and retrospective storytelling are debated.
famous_dreams.source_title: Historical accounts of Kekulé’s benzene story should be presented cautiously.

famous_dreams.title: Dmitri Mendeleev
famous_dreams.claim: A popular story says Mendeleev saw the periodic arrangement in a dream.
famous_dreams.status: Widely repeated anecdote; the table also followed years of documented work, so the dream should not be portrayed as its sole origin.

famous_dreams.title: Elias Howe
famous_dreams.claim: A later story says Howe dreamed of spear-carrying attackers whose spear points suggested placing the sewing-machine needle’s eye near its tip.
famous_dreams.status: Popular but poorly documented story; label as folklore or disputed, not established fact.

famous_dreams.title: Mary Shelley
famous_dreams.claim: In her 1831 introduction to Frankenstein, Shelley described a vivid waking dream of the creator and creature that supplied the central image of the story.
famous_dreams.status: Strong first-person evidence, written years after the 1816 event.

famous_dreams.title: Paul McCartney
famous_dreams.claim: McCartney has repeatedly said that the melody that became “Yesterday” came to him in a dream; he initially checked that he had not unconsciously remembered someone else’s tune.
famous_dreams.status: First-person account repeated in interviews and biographies.
famous_dreams.source_title: Paul McCartney’s account of composing Yesterday

famous_dreams.title: Otto Loewi
famous_dreams.claim: Loewi reported that an experimental idea came to him during sleep, was forgotten, returned the next night, and led to work demonstrating chemical transmission of nerve impulses.
famous_dreams.status: First-person scientific recollection; the discovery was recognized with the 1936 Nobel Prize shared with Henry Dale.
famous_dreams.source_title: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1936
